skills.title: Indigenous Nations Before 1713
skills.description: Many Indigenous nations, like the Wendat, Mi'kmaq, Cree, and Inuit, met Europeans long ago. Match each nation to where it lived and how it lived.

skills.title: First Nations Before Europeans Came
skills.description: Before Europeans arrived, First Nations and Inuit traded, made alliances, and sometimes competed for waterways. Sort examples into working together or competing.

skills.title: Why Europeans Came
skills.description: Explorers like Cabot, Cartier, and Champlain came for fur, fish, land, and to spread their religion. Match each person or group to why they came.

skills.title: Who Mattered in New France
skills.description: New France had a king, a governor, a bishop, an intendant, priests, nuns, and the seigneurial system. Match each one to what it did for settlers.

skills.title: Meeting of Peoples
skills.description: Indigenous peoples and Europeans traded, shared skills, made alliances, and sometimes fought. Match each kind of interaction to an example.

skills.title: How the Métis People Began
skills.description: The Métis people grew from fur traders and First Nations families in places like the Great Lakes and Mattawa. Pick the reasons that led to this.

skills.title: Indigenous and European Differences
skills.description: Indigenous and European communities differed in how they were governed, used land, and shared work. Match each difference to its reason.

skills.title: European Wars and Indigenous Peoples
skills.description: When France and Britain fought, First Nations were pulled in and control of places like Acadia changed. Match each conflict to its effects.

skills.title: Good and Bad Results of Contact
skills.description: Contact brought alliances and new ideas, but also sickness, lost land, and alcohol. Sort the results into positive or negative.

skills.title: Who Gained From Whom
skills.description: Europeans gained knowledge of the land, food, and trade routes, while First Nations gained new tools and materials. Match each gain to who got it.

skills.title: Early Contact and Canada Today
skills.description: Long-ago events link to today's land claims, treaty rights, and caring for the land. Match each past event to the issue it connects to.

skills.title: Rights and Duties of Citizens
skills.description: Canadians have rights like voting and free speech, and duties like respecting others. Sort each one into a right or a responsibility.

skills.title: Levels of Government
skills.description: Federal, provincial, territorial, and municipal governments, band councils, and school boards each run different services. Match each to what it looks after.

skills.title: Indigenous Governments Today
skills.description: First Nations, Métis, and Inuit have their own groups, like the Métis Nation of Ontario and the Haudenosaunee Confederacy. Match each group to who it speaks for.

skills.title: Governments Sharing the Job
skills.description: Some services, like health care and transportation, are shared by several levels of government. Match each job to the governments that share it.

skills.title: How Governments Ask the Public
skills.description: Governments ask people what they think through elections, town halls, and public hearings. Match each way to how it works and why asking matters.

skills.title: Duty to Consult Indigenous Peoples
skills.description: Governments must talk with First Nations, Métis, and Inuit before projects like pipelines or mines affect their land. Pick the times this duty applies.

skills.title: What Governments Do About Problems
skills.description: Governments make laws and programs, like recycling programs and language projects, to fix problems. Match each action to the problem it solves.

skills.title: Why Views on Issues Differ
skills.description: Farmers, companies, governments, and environmentalists can see the same issue differently. Match each group to its likely view and why.

skills.title: How Citizens Take Action
skills.description: People can sign petitions, vote, volunteer, write letters, or boycott to help fix problems. Pick the action that fits each situation.

skills.title: Did the Government Action Work?
skills.description: We can judge whether a government action helped solve a problem, like clean water or housing. Pick the signs that show it worked or did not.

skills.title: Plans to Fix Problems
skills.description: A good plan for a social or environmental problem says what governments will do and what citizens will do. Sort the steps into government jobs and citizen jobs.
